quotes.text: The most likely candidates, according to materials used in Lehi's day, would be animal skins, clay, wood covered with wax, or possibly papyrus. The Talmud specified the use of the skins of clean animals for writing the law, and the Hebrews were expert at dressing skins (see Exodus 25:5; Leviticus 13:48). Rolls, or scrolls, made from skins were used in Lehi's day (see Jeremiah 36:2; Ezekiel 2:9-10).

Although in verse 29 the Lord mentions an earlier prophecy which the king had questioned, this is the only prophecy that is actually recorded in this chapter. It really consists of three prophecies. First, Jehoiakim is told that no son of his will sit upon the throne of David. Jehoiachin, the son of Jehoiakim, did succeed his father, but he was only eighteen years of age (see 2 Kings 24:8; 2 Chronicles 36:9 says he was only eight, but this is obviously an error for he had children), and he reigned only three months and ten days. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had captured his father Jehoiakim and carried him bound into Babylon, later sending for Jehoiachin and appointing Zedekiah as the puppet king in Judah (see 2 Chronicles 36:5-10). Jehoiachin may not have been officially recognized as a king by the Lord or by Jeremiah, and he certainly was not by Nebuchadnezzar.

quotes.text: There are no dates identifying when the relations in the first twenty chapters of Jeremiah were given. is possible that these twenty chapters, along with the prophecies concerning the surrounding nations (chapters 46 through ), constituted the first compilation which Jehoiakim cut up with a penknife. Since they were all compiled at once, the ting would not seem important; but all of them preceded the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Revelations added later were dated.
